title: Rent in Every Major City vs the Salary You Need

scenes.narration: To rent a normal one-bedroom apartment in New York City today, landlords want you to earn about a hundred and sixty thousand dollars a year. For the same apartment in a cheaper major city, the number can be under forty thousand. Same four walls, same single bedroom — and a salary requirement that swings by four times depending only on the city. Today we rank what rent costs in every major city, and the salary you'd need to actually afford it.

Here's the rule quietly running your life. Most landlords require your annual income to be at least forty times the monthly rent — which is the same as saying rent should eat no more than thirty percent of your pay. Flip it around, and every rent price hides a salary you must earn just to be allowed through the door.
scenes.sub: income landlords require vs the monthly rent

scenes.narration: So today we rank major cities by rent, convert each one into the salary you'd actually need, expose the thirty-percent rule landlords enforce, map where renters are most crushed, and reveal where your paycheck buys the most roof. Because rent isn't just a bill. It's an invisible salary requirement stamped on every city.

scenes.memeTop: live in the city you love
scenes.memeBottom: live in a city you can afford
scenes.narration: Because for millions of renters, this is the real monthly decision — the dream city, or the affordable one. Before we rank them, let's nail down the one rule that turns any rent into a salary.
First, the rule that turns rent into a required salary.
scenes.heading: The 30% Rule

scenes.caption: rent should take no more than ~30% of pay
scenes.narration: The anchor is simple: housing should cost no more than about thirty percent of your gross income. Cross that line and you're officially rent-burdened, with too little left for everything else. Landlords turn the same rule into a wall — most won't even rent to you unless you earn forty times the monthly rent. That's the thirty-percent rule, enforced.

And the thirty-percent line isn't arbitrary — it's the point where a budget starts to crack. Below it, you can save, handle a surprise, and build a life. Above it, one broken car or missed shift can mean a missed rent payment. That single line separates renters who are building a future from renters who are just surviving the month.

And renting is its own kind of contract. It's an agreement where you pay to use property owned by someone else, with a signed lease to establish the roles and expectations of both the tenant and landlord. You're not buying a home — you're buying time in it, month by month, at whatever price the local market sets.

And a lease is a promise with teeth. Sign a twelve-month lease and you owe every month of it, whether you stay or not. Break it early and you can forfeit your deposit or owe the balance. That's why the salary question matters so much up front: you're not committing to one month of rent, you're committing to a year of it.

props.name: ballchain
props.label: owe it even if you leave

scenes.narration: And notice the rule is measured against gross income — the sum of your earnings before any deductions or taxes. That's the catch landlords rarely mention: they test you on your pre-tax salary, but you pay rent out of your take-home. So the real bite on your actual paycheck is always even bigger than thirty percent.

And here's the quiet trap inside that gross-income rule. A city with high rent usually has high taxes too, so your take-home shrinks exactly where rent grows. The listing tests your pre-tax salary, but the rent comes out of what's left after the government's cut. On a real paycheck, thirty percent gross can easily be forty percent of what you actually bring home.
So let's rank the cities by raw monthly rent.
scenes.heading: The Rent

scenes.caption: median one-bed rent, by major city
scenes.narration: Here's the monthly damage for a typical one-bedroom. New York leads near four thousand dollars a month. San Francisco and the glamour cities aren't far behind. The pricey-but-sane tier sits around two thousand. And affordable boomtowns still land near fourteen or fifteen hundred. Between the top and the bottom of this list is a threefold gap — for the exact same apartment.

And these are just the asking rents — the number on the listing. The real cost of landing an apartment in a hot city includes bidding wars, where desperate renters offer months of rent up front just to win the unit. In the tightest markets, the advertised price is the floor of what you'll actually pay, not the ceiling.

scenes.title: Median 1-bed rent per month ($)
scenes.narration: Put the numbers side by side. New York around four thousand a month, San Francisco thirty-three hundred, Miami near twenty-eight, Chicago about two thousand, Austin seventeen hundred, Houston closer to fourteen. The most expensive city charges nearly three times the cheapest — for four walls and a single bedroom in each.

Stack it up over a year and the gap is staggering. A New York renter pays nearly thirty thousand dollars more per year than a Houston renter — for the same one-bedroom. Over a decade, that's a quarter of a million dollars, gone to a landlord, that the cheaper-city renter could have invested instead.
scenes.sub: NYC vs Houston rent gap — same 1-bed

scenes.narration: But a raw rent number is only half the story. Four thousand a month is punishing on an average salary and trivial on a huge one. The honest way to compare cities isn't the rent itself — it's the salary that rent silently demands. So let's convert every one of these prices into the income you'd need to clear the door.

Here's the whole trick in one line. Multiply any monthly rent by forty and you get the salary a landlord wants you to earn. Four thousand a month? A hundred and sixty thousand a year. Memorize that one multiplication and you can read the true price of any city the instant you see a listing.
So here's the number nobody puts on the listing.
scenes.heading: The Salary Needed

scenes.caption: income required to rent, by city
scenes.narration: Run every rent through the forty-times rule and the cities transform into salary requirements. New York demands around a hundred and sixty thousand a year to rent a basic one-bed. San Francisco, roughly a hundred and thirty. Even the mid-tier cities quietly require six figures. The affordable ones ask fifty to seventy thousand. The apartment didn't change. The salary to unlock it did.

And flip the rule to protect yourself. Whatever you earn, divide by forty to find the highest rent you can truly carry. Earn eighty thousand? Your ceiling is two thousand a month. It feels brutal in an expensive city, but that line is the difference between a home that funds your life and one that quietly consumes it.

scenes.title: Salary needed to rent a 1-bed ($K/yr)
scenes.narration: Here it is in black and white. To rent that one-bedroom, New York wants about a hundred and sixty thousand a year, San Francisco a hundred and thirty, Miami over a hundred, Chicago around eighty, Austin near seventy, Houston in the mid-fifties. These aren't luxury numbers — they're the price of a single ordinary bedroom in each city.

And remember, this is the salary for just one bedroom. Add a partner who also needs space, or kids who need their own rooms, and the required income climbs fast. A family that wants a modest two or three bedrooms in a top city can need a quarter of a million dollars a year just to clear the rent rule.

Now compare that to what people actually earn. The median worker in most of these cities makes nowhere near the salary their own rent requires. In New York, the income needed to rent comfortably is roughly double the city's median wage. The math simply doesn't close — which is why so many renters are quietly drowning.

Here's the gap that breaks the system. In many top cities, the salary a landlord requires to rent a one-bedroom is nearly double what the typical worker there actually earns. The people who keep the city running simply cannot, on paper, qualify to rent in it. That's not a glitch — it's the whole crisis in one number.
scenes.sub: salary needed vs what the median worker earns

scenes.narration: Which is why a word has quietly taken over housing: rent-burdened.
scenes.heading: Rent-Burdened

scenes.caption: renters paying over 30% of income on rent
scenes.narration: When rent crosses thirty percent of your income, you're rent-burdened. Cross fifty percent and you're severely rent-burdened. In the priciest cities, the majority of renters are now over that first line, and a huge share are over the second — handing more than half of every paycheck to a landlord before they've eaten, commuted, or saved a single dollar.

And rent burden quietly steals your future, not just your month. Every extra dollar handed to a landlord is a dollar that never becomes savings, investments, or a down payment. The severely burdened renter isn't just poorer today — they're locked out of ever building the wealth that would let them escape renting at all.

Economists track this with a housing affordability index, which measures the degree to which the median person or family can actually afford local housing. When that index collapses, it's not a statistic — it's roommates into your thirties, three jobs to make rent, and a whole generation priced out of the cities built for them.

And the burden falls hardest on exactly the people a city needs most. Teachers, nurses, baristas, and artists — the workers who make a city run — are the first to be priced out when rent outruns wages. A city that no one but bankers can afford to rent in slowly loses the very people who made it worth living in.

And rent burden is uniquely vicious because it never stops. A mortgage is mostly fixed and eventually ends. Rent renews every single year, usually upward, for as long as you live there. The rent-burdened renter isn't climbing toward anything — they're running in place, paying more each year for the exact same room.

And the burden is spreading fast. Across the biggest US cities, roughly half of all renters now spend more than thirty percent of their income on rent, and about a quarter spend more than half. Being rent-burdened used to be a crisis. In the priciest cities, it's quietly become the norm.
scenes.sub: of big-city renters are now rent-burdened

scenes.narration: So why is rent in these cities so insane in the first place?
scenes.heading: Why So High

scenes.narration: The oldest attempted fix is rent control — a system of laws for the rental market of dwellings that caps how fast rent can rise. It genuinely protects the people already in those apartments. But economists widely argue it also discourages new building and shrinks supply over time, which can quietly make the shortage — and the prices for everyone else — even worse.

scenes.memeTop: half my paycheck to a landlord
scenes.narration: For the severely rent-burdened, this is the monthly mood: more than half the paycheck gone before anything else, and a quiet acceptance that this is just how it is now. It isn't how it has to be — but only if you treat rent as the salary test it really is.

The deeper cause is the same one behind every housing crisis: too many people chasing too few homes. The most desirable cities simply don't build enough apartments for everyone who wants in. Scarcity hands landlords the power to name their price — and in a city everyone's fighting to live in, that price only goes one direction.

And wages are the other half of the equation everyone ignores. Rent can only rise as far as it does because, in the richest cities, enough high earners exist to pay it. Their big salaries set the market price — and everyone earning a normal wage is forced to compete against a banker's paycheck for the same one-bedroom.
And the same rent buys wildly different lives.
scenes.heading: What Rent Buys

scenes.caption: the same rent, a closet or a house
scenes.narration: Take two thousand dollars a month. In New York or San Francisco, that's a room in a shared apartment, maybe a tiny studio if you're lucky. In an affordable city, the same two thousand rents a spacious two-bedroom with parking and a yard. Identical money, and the roof over your head quadruples in size.

Say the location premium out loud. The same two-thousand-dollar budget rents a shared room in Manhattan or an entire two-bedroom house with a yard in an affordable city. You're not paying for more space in the expensive city — you're paying purely for the zip code. The walls are smaller; only the address is bigger.
scenes.sub: a shared room, or a whole house — same money

scenes.narration: So what should a renter actually do with all this?
scenes.heading: What To Do

scenes.narration: First, know your real number before you ever tour a place. Multiply your gross salary by thirty percent, divide by twelve — that's your true monthly ceiling. If a city's median rent sits above that line, you're not underpaid, you're in the wrong city for your income. Run the number first, fall in love second.

And audit the rent you already pay. Most renters never run their own thirty-percent number, then wonder why money evaporates. Pull up your lease, divide the rent by your monthly take-home, and look at the real percentage. If it's well over a third, you've found the leak draining your entire budget — and the biggest single thing you can fix.

Second, attack the biggest rent with the oldest trick: split it. A roommate often cuts your single biggest expense in half instantly — no raise, no move required. In the priciest cities, sharing isn't failure, it's math. One roommate can be the difference between rent-burdened and actually saving money.

And treat rent as temporary, not permanent. The goal for most people is to rent lean, invest the gap, and eventually trade rising rent for a fixed mortgage that ends. A renter who keeps costs down and buys when the math works turns today's discipline into tomorrow's paid-off home.

Third, if your job travels, let your rent travel with it. Earning a big-city salary while renting in a cheaper city is the single fastest downgrade to your biggest bill. You don't need a raise to feel richer — you need a zip code where the rent stops demanding a six-figure salary for one bedroom.

And time your move to the market, not your mood. Rents swing with the seasons — winter is quiet and cheap, summer is a feeding frenzy. Signing a lease in the slow months, or renewing early before a hike, can lock in hundreds less a month. The same apartment has a different price depending only on when you sign.

Because here's the real lesson. Every rent price is really a salary requirement in disguise, and most people discover theirs only after the city has already broken their budget. Read the requirement first. Rank your cities by the income their rent silently demands — and refuse to let a single bedroom quietly set the entire course of your financial life.

And zoom out on the decades. A renter who keeps housing near thirty percent and invests the difference can retire comfortably. One who lets rent creep to half their income, in a city they couldn't really afford, may never catch up. The rent you choose today quietly writes the size of the life you'll be able to afford later.
